notes: Slot 1 = Republican Party (Nixon, ruling) and slot 2 = Democratic Party as required by the focus tree. Conservative Coalition of Southern Democrats in 14 (carries 0.10 popularity). Black Panther Party in 7 (anti-Western revolutionary vanguard with Algiers/Pyongyang ties); John Birch Society in 6 as reactionary anti-establishment right. Libertarian slot 16 starts with the Society for Individual Liberty (1969) and switches to the Libertarian Party on 1971.12.11. MD sprites used only where the same organization (GOP, Democrats, CPUSA, NOI, WWP, Socialist Party, Libertarian Party, armed forces).

0.name: Central Intelligence Agency
0.text:
The Central Intelligence Agency was created by the National Security Act of 1947 and is directed since 1966 by Richard Helms. It runs a secret war in Laos, the Phoenix programme in South Vietnam, and covert operations against leftist movements from Chile to the Congo, accountable only to a handful of congressmen.

The Agency sees the Cold War as a global contest in which allied dictators, military juntas and secret funding of parties, unions and newspapers are legitimate tools against Soviet influence. Its leverage lies in its budget hidden in the defence accounts, its access to the President and its reputation as the indispensable guardian of American power abroad.

1.name: Republican Party
1.text:
The Republican Party, founded in 1854, returned to the White House in January 1969 when Richard Nixon narrowly defeated Hubert Humphrey. Nixon governs with Democratic majorities in both houses of Congress, relying on Vice President Spiro Agnew to attack the press and antiwar protesters on behalf of what he calls the silent majority.

The party combines Eisenhower-style moderates, Goldwater conservatives and a growing Southern wing courted through the Southern strategy. Nixon pursues Vietnamization and gradual troop withdrawals, détente with Moscow and an opening toward Beijing, while promising law and order at home. Its base lies in the suburbs, small towns, business and the Sun Belt.

2.name: Democratic Party
2.text:
The Democratic Party, the oldest party in the United States, lost the presidency in 1968 after Lyndon Johnson withdrew and the Chicago convention ended in riots, but it still controls Congress under Speaker John McCormack and Senate Majority Leader Mike Mansfield. National chairman Fred Harris oversees the McGovern Commission's reform of delegate selection.

The party is a coalition of New Deal labour unions, big-city machines, Black voters, liberal intellectuals and the conservative Solid South, now torn apart by Vietnam and civil rights. Its liberal wing demands withdrawal from Indochina and an expanded Great Society. Its leverage lies in its congressional majorities and the governorships and city halls it holds.

3.name: Socialist Party of America
3.text:
The Socialist Party of America, founded in 1901 and once led by Eugene Debs and Norman Thomas, is now a small organisation chaired by Michael Harrington, author of The Other America, with Bayard Rustin among its prominent members. It no longer runs its own presidential candidates.

The party pursues a realignment strategy: working inside the Democratic Party and the labour movement to build an American social democracy based on full employment, national health insurance and civil rights. It is firmly anti-communist and divided over Vietnam. Its leverage lies in intellectual influence, ties to the AFL-CIO leadership and the civil rights coalition.

4.name: Communist Party USA
4.text:
The Communist Party USA was founded in 1919 and is led by General Secretary Gus Hall. Decimated by McCarthyism and Khrushchev's revelations of 1956, it remains the most loyal pro-Soviet party in the West, having endorsed the 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia. The young philosopher Angela Davis, a member since 1968, was dismissed by the University of California in 1969.

The party calls for peace in Vietnam, Black liberation, trade union militancy and socialism on the Soviet model. It is funded secretly from Moscow and infiltrated by the FBI. Its leverage lies in its disciplined cadre, its presence in peace and civil rights coalitions and its role as the voice of the Soviet line in America.

5.name: Students for a Democratic Society
5.text:
Students for a Democratic Society, founded in 1960, became the leading organisation of the New Left and the campus antiwar movement. At its June 1969 convention it split between the Maoist Progressive Labor faction and the Weatherman faction of Bernardine Dohrn, Mark Rudd and Bill Ayers, which staged the Days of Rage in Chicago and in December 1969 resolved to go underground.

What remains of SDS preaches revolution against American imperialism, solidarity with the Vietnamese and Black liberation movements and the destruction of the system by direct action. It rejects both parties and the Soviet model. Its leverage lies in campus networks of hundreds of thousands of radicalised students.

6.name: John Birch Society
6.text:
The John Birch Society was founded in 1958 by the candy manufacturer Robert Welch and is based in Belmont, Massachusetts. Shunned by William F. Buckley and mainstream conservatives, it still counts tens of thousands of members in local chapters, bookstores and front committees across the country.

The Society believes the federal government, the foreign policy establishment and the civil rights movement are penetrated by a communist conspiracy. It demands that the United States get out of the United Nations, opposes foreign aid, détente and the federal income tax, and calls for victory or withdrawal in Vietnam. Its leverage lies in grassroots activism and influence over local school boards and Republican clubs.

7.name: Black Panther Party
7.text:
The Black Panther Party was founded in Oakland in 1966 by Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale. Newton is in prison, Seale faces trial in Chicago, Minister of Information Eldridge Cleaver runs an international section in Algiers, and in December 1969 Chicago police killed Fred Hampton in his bed. The FBI calls the party the greatest threat to internal security.

The Panthers combine Marxism-Leninism with Black nationalism, demanding self-defence against police, community control and an end to the war. They run free breakfast programmes and clinics and seek alliances with Algeria, North Korea, Cuba and North Vietnam. Their leverage lies in armed discipline and the loyalty of young Black Americans in the cities.

8.name: Islamic Center of America
8.text:
The Islamic Center of America was opened in Detroit in 1963 by Imam Mohammad Jawad Chirri, a Lebanese Shia scholar who serves the Arab community of Detroit and Dearborn, many of them from south Lebanon and working in the Ford plants. It is the largest Shia institution in the country.

The Center teaches that Islam is compatible with American citizenship and democracy, promotes education, interfaith dialogue and the integration of immigrant families, and keeps ties to Lebanese clerics such as Musa al-Sadr. It supports the Palestinian cause but avoids partisan politics. Its leverage lies in a growing community of autoworkers and merchants and in respect from Detroit politicians.

9.name: Muslim Students' Association Persian-Speaking Group
9.text:
The Persian-Speaking Group of the Muslim Students' Association is a network of Iranian students and professionals in the United States who oppose the Shah from an Islamic standpoint. The Texas-based pharmacologist Ebrahim Yazdi, a leader of the exiled Freedom Movement of Iran, is among its organisers and maintains contact with Ayatollah Khomeini in Najaf.

The group holds that the Shah's monarchy is an American puppet that betrays Islam and Iran's oil wealth, and it circulates Khomeini's lectures on government by the jurist. It rejects both American imperialism and atheist communism. Its leverage lies in thousands of Iranian students on American campuses and its links to clerical opposition in Iran.

10.name: Muslim Students' Association
10.text:
The Muslim Students' Association of the United States and Canada was founded in 1963 at the University of Illinois by foreign Muslim students, many from the Arab world, Pakistan and India. It has chapters at dozens of universities and receives support from Saudi Arabia and the Muslim World League.

The association promotes Sunni orthodoxy, prayer facilities, halal food and the publication of Islamic literature, while avoiding confrontation with American authorities. It favours solidarity with Muslim states, especially Saudi Arabia, and the Palestinian cause. Its leverage lies in its foreign funding, its educated membership and its role as the main national Muslim organisation outside the Nation of Islam.

11.name: Dar ul-Islam Movement
11.text:
The Dar ul-Islam Movement was founded in 1962 at the State Street Mosque in Brooklyn by African-American converts to Sunni Islam, among them Imam Yahya Abdul-Karim. It is spreading through mosques in New York, Philadelphia, Cleveland and the prisons, where it competes with the Nation of Islam.

The movement seeks to build self-governing Islamic communities under sharia in the heart of the American city, under an imam whose authority members accept in place of secular law. It rejects the Nation of Islam's racial theology, American capitalism and the state as un-Islamic. Its leverage lies in disciplined communities, a security arm and its appeal to Black prisoners and veterans.

12.name: Nation of Islam
12.text:
The Nation of Islam was founded in Detroit in 1930 and has been led from Chicago since 1934 by Elijah Muhammad. Despite the assassination of Malcolm X in 1965 it continues to grow, with temples in most large cities, Louis Farrakhan as its national spokesman and Muhammad Ali as its most famous member.

The Nation preaches Black self-reliance, moral discipline and racial separation, and demands land for a separate Black nation. It builds businesses, farms, schools and the newspaper Muhammad Speaks, and refuses military service in what it calls the white man's wars. Its leverage lies in its economic enterprises, its disciplined Fruit of Islam and its following in the ghettos and prisons.

13.name: Federal Bureau of Investigation
13.text:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation has been led since 1924 by J. Edgar Hoover, who has turned it into an autonomous power that presidents fear to challenge. Through its secret COINTELPRO programmes it infiltrates and disrupts the Communist Party, the Black Panthers, the New Left and the civil rights movement, while keeping files on politicians of both parties.

The Bureau sees itself as the guardian of order, morality and internal security against subversion of every kind, answerable in practice to no one but its director. It distrusts the CIA and liberal reformers alike. Its leverage lies in its files, its public image of incorruptibility and Hoover's network of allies in Congress.

14.name: Conservative Coalition
14.text:
The Conservative Coalition is the informal congressional alliance of Southern Democrats and conservative Republicans that has shaped legislation since the late 1930s. Its Senate pillars include Richard Russell of Georgia, now president pro tempore, James Eastland of Mississippi and John Stennis, who command key committee chairmanships through seniority.

The coalition defends states' rights, balanced budgets, a strong military and the agricultural interests of the South and Midwest, and it resisted civil rights and Great Society legislation. Its members are hawks on Vietnam but suspicious of federal power at home. Its leverage lies in seniority, the filibuster and the swing votes it controls in a closely divided Congress.

15.name: Business Council
15.text:
The Business Council began in 1933 as an advisory body to the Department of Commerce and became independent in the early 1960s. Its members are the chief executives of the largest American corporations, including General Motors, AT&T, General Electric, US Steel and the great New York banks, who meet regularly with cabinet officers behind closed doors.

The Council favours free trade, stable labour relations, low inflation, a strong dollar and an open world economy anchored by American power. It supports containment of communism but increasingly worries about the costs of Vietnam. Its leverage lies in its members' control of capital, jobs and campaign finance, and their easy access to the White House.

16.name: Society for Individual Liberty
16.text:
The Society for Individual Liberty was formed in 1969 by Don Ernsberger and Dave Walter after libertarians broke with Young Americans for Freedom at its stormy St. Louis convention, where draft-card burning split the conservative youth movement. It links campus libertarian alliances and readers of Ayn Rand and Murray Rothbard.

The Society calls for an end to conscription, the war and drug laws, abolition of income tax and the welfare state, and a free market without government subsidy. It rejects both conservatism and the New Left. Its leverage lies in a young, intellectually energetic following and its ability to publish and organise among disaffected students.

16.name: Libertarian Party
16.text:
The Libertarian Party is founded in December 1971 in Colorado Springs at the home of David Nolan, after Nixon's wage and price controls and the end of the gold standard convince a group of libertarian activists that neither major party defends economic freedom.

The party stands for minimal government, free markets, an end to the draft and military interventions, drug legalisation and civil liberties. It rejects both the welfare state and the warfare state. Its base is small, made up of students, engineers, small entrepreneurs and readers of Ayn Rand, but it aims to contest elections nationwide and build a permanent third party.

17.name: Sierra Club
17.text:
The Sierra Club was founded in 1892 by John Muir and has grown under David Brower into the most militant conservation organisation in the country before the board forced him out in 1969; Michael McCloskey is now executive director. The National Environmental Policy Act, signed on 1 January 1970, owes much to its campaigning.

The Club fights dams in the Grand Canyon, logging of redwoods, oil drilling and pollution, and supports new national parks and wilderness areas. It is non-partisan and avoids foreign policy. Its leverage lies in a rapidly growing membership, legal action, full-page newspaper advertising and public alarm about the environment ahead of the first Earth Day.

18.name: Peace and Freedom Party
18.text:
The Peace and Freedom Party was founded in California in 1967 by antiwar activists who gathered enough signatures to qualify for the ballot. In 1968 it allied with the Black Panther Party and nominated Eldridge Cleaver for president, and it now runs candidates in California and several other states.

The party calls for immediate withdrawal from Vietnam, socialism through democratic means, community control of police, Black liberation and an end to poverty. It rejects both the Democratic Party's cold war liberalism and Soviet-style communism. Its leverage lies in its ballot line, its appeal to radical students and its role as a bridge between the white left and Black radicals.

19.name: Workers World Party
19.text:
The Workers World Party was founded in 1959 by Sam Marcy and supporters who left the Trotskyist Socialist Workers Party, having backed the Soviet intervention in Hungary in 1956. Its youth group, Youth Against War and Fascism, is prominent in street demonstrations against the Vietnam War.

The party supports all anti-imperialist states and movements, from North Vietnam and North Korea to China and Cuba, without subordinating itself to Moscow or Beijing. It calls for socialist revolution, Black and Puerto Rican self-determination and solidarity with prisoners and soldiers. Its leverage lies in a small but disciplined cadre able to organise militant protests.

20.name: American Independent Party
20.text:
The American Independent Party was founded in California in 1967 to carry the presidential campaign of Governor George Wallace of Alabama, who in 1968 won five Southern states and 13.5 per cent of the national vote. Wallace is now preparing to reclaim the Alabama governorship in 1970 as a springboard for another national campaign.

The party campaigns against forced busing, federal civil rights enforcement, pointy-headed bureaucrats, antiwar protesters and urban riots, promising law and order and states' rights. It wants victory in Vietnam or withdrawal. Its leverage lies in white working-class voters in the South and the industrial North who feel abandoned by both major parties.

21.name: National States' Rights Party
21.text:
The National States' Rights Party was founded in 1958 by J. B. Stoner and Edward Reed Fields and is based in Georgia, where it publishes the newspaper The Thunderbolt. It is the largest openly white-supremacist party in the South, with links to Klan groups and a long record of violence against the civil rights movement.

The party preaches antisemitism, racial segregation and white nationalism, borrowing symbols from German National Socialism. It demands the deportation of Black Americans and denounces both parties as tools of a Jewish-communist conspiracy. Its leverage is small but menacing: armed members, rallies in Southern towns and the ability to exploit racial tension.

22.name: Joint Chiefs of Staff
22.text:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff are the heads of the Army, Navy, Air Force and Marine Corps, chaired by General Earle Wheeler. They command a military of more than three million men, with nearly half a million still in South Vietnam, and depend on a draft that since December 1969 is decided by lottery.

The chiefs press for a free hand in Indochina, including bombing of sanctuaries in Cambodia and Laos, and resist cuts in strategic forces during arms control talks. They are loyal to civilian authority but frustrated by limited war and public hostility. Their leverage lies in the defence budget, industry and congressional allies, and their authority in matters of national security.

23.name: Friends of the Crown
23.text:
Friends of the Crown is a small circle of Anglophile antiquarians, Episcopalian traditionalists and descendants of colonial loyalist families in New England, Virginia and New York. It meets in clubs and historical societies, celebrates the Queen's birthday and has no public leader.

The circle regards the Revolution as an unfortunate family quarrel and argues that a hereditary head of state above party would have spared America the bitter partisanship, riots and assassinations of the 1960s. It favours ever closer ties with Britain and the Commonwealth and an ordered, hierarchical society. Its leverage is nil beyond old money, social prestige and a romantic following.
